questions.question: The lecture was so ________ that students who had come expecting to be challenged left with nothing more than a list of platitudes.
options: trenchant
vapid
abstruse
incisive
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: The word 'vapid' means lacking flavor, zest, or substance; dull and flat. The context clues indicate that students left with 'nothing more than a list of platitudes' (clichés/empty remarks), which directly matches a lecture lacking intellectual substance ('vapid'). 'Trenchant' and 'incisive' mean vigorous, sharp, or keen, while 'abstruse' means difficult to understand—none of which align with leaving with empty platitudes.

questions.question: Though the critics were ________ in their praise of the debut, the author remained wary, having seen how quickly enthusiasm could curdle into contempt.
options: effusive
tepid
guarded
cursory
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: The author remained wary because enthusiasm could easily 'curdle into contempt', implying that the initial praise was extreme, unrestrained, or lavish. 'Effusive' means expressing feelings of gratitude, pleasure, or approval in an unrestrained or heartfelt manner. 'Tepid' means showing little enthusiasm, which contradicts the author's worry about excessive enthusiasm turning sour.

questions.question: The reformer's zeal was ________ by a stubborn pragmatism, so that for all his fiery speeches he never proposed a measure that could not pass.
options: stoked
amplified
tempered
ignited
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: The sentence contrasts his 'fiery speeches' (zeal) with his practical limitation that 'he never proposed a measure that could not pass'. This means his enthusiasm was restrained or moderated by reality. 'Tempered' means to act as a neutralizing or controlling element to something (moderated), making it the exact fit.

questions.question: While the new app was praised as innovative, its poor security turned out to be its ________, and users abandoned it within weeks.
options: golden goose
Trojan horse
Achilles' heel
lion's share
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: The context describes a fatal weakness in an otherwise strong creation that led users to abandon it. An 'Achilles' heel' refers to a weakness or vulnerable point in an otherwise strong system or person, causing ultimate failure.

questions.question: The CEO's ________ optimism contrasted sharply with the ________ mood on the shop floor, where rumours of layoffs had made workers ________.
options: unwarranted; despondent; apprehensive
justified; buoyant; relaxed
feigned; jubilant; anxious
tepid; hopeful; assured
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: Rumours of layoffs naturally create a gloomy and fearful atmosphere among workers ('despondent' mood and 'apprehensive' workers). In contrast, a CEO ignoring this reality displays 'unwarranted' optimism, forming a sharp contrast.

questions.question: Having ________ the evidence for years, the historian was ________ to find that the archive's newest document ________ her central thesis.
options: scrutinised; delighted; undermined
neglected; relieved; refuted
catalogued; gratified; undermined
scrutinised; dismayed; undermined
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: If a historian has spent years carefully looking at evidence ('scrutinised'), finding a new document that destroys her life's work ('undermined her central thesis') would naturally cause shock and disappointment ('dismayed'). Option 3 uses 'delighted', which contradicts finding your thesis destroyed.

questions.question: Rather than ________ the dispute, the court's ruling merely ________ it, leaving both parties at liberty to ________ the same arguments.
options: settle; postponed; repeat
worsen; resolved; abandon
ignore; escalated; forget
settle; ended; revive
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: The contrast word 'Rather than' implies that instead of resolving or finishing the issue ('settle'), the ruling delayed it ('postponed'), which gives the parties freedom to bring up the same points again ('repeat').

questions.question: The poet's late work, once dismissed as ________, is now admired for the very ________ that earlier critics ________.
options: lucid; clarity; deplored
obscure; simplicity; admired
trivial; depth; praised
obscure; density; deplored
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: A shift in critical appreciation usually means something previously criticized is now praised. If it was dismissed for being hard to understand ('obscure'), it is now admired for that same heavy complexity ('density') which critics earlier condemned ('deplored').

questions.question: The explorer's account was ________ with exaggeration, but later expeditions ________ its broad outline while ________ many of its details.
options: free; contradicted; retaining
riddled; confirmed; discarding
devoid; verified; embellishing
laden; refuted; preserving
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: An account full of exaggeration ('riddled' with it) can still hold general truth; later expeditions verified the main structure ('confirmed') while throwing out false small components ('discarding').

questions.question: The report, along with its appendices, <u>were</u> submitted to the board on Friday.
options: have been
are
being
was
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: Expressions introduced by phrases like 'along with', 'together with', or 'accompanied by' do not change the grammatical number of the subject. The subject is 'The report' (singular), so the verb must be singular: 'was'.

questions.question: No sooner had the results been announced <u>when</u> protests broke out.
options: then
that
as
than
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: Correlative conjunction pairs are fixed in English grammar. The correlative partner for 'No sooner' is always 'than' (just as 'Scarcely' or 'Hardly' is followed by 'when').

questions.question: She is one of those leaders who <u>inspires</u> loyalty without demanding it.
options: is inspiring
has inspired
inspire
inspiring
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: In the structure 'one of those plural nouns who...', the relative pronoun 'who' refers back to the plural noun 'leaders', not 'one'. Therefore, the verb following 'who' must be plural: 'inspire'.

questions.question: The committee was <u>comprised of</u> eight members drawn from three universities.
options: comprising of
composed of
comprised by
composing of
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: The active verb 'comprise' means 'to include' or 'to consist of' (the whole comprises parts). It cannot take 'of' in the passive voice unless rephrased as 'is composed of' or 'consists of'. Thus, 'composed of' is grammatically accurate.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: The athlete's candid admission of her doubts endeared her to the public.
The new law abrogates the ministry's right to appoint its own officials.
His prodigal savings ensured a comfortable retirement.
The prosecutor's insinuations were only thinly veiled, and the jury noticed.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: 'Prodigal' means spending money or resources freely and recklessly; wastefully extravagant. It makes no sense to talk about 'prodigal savings' ensuring a secure retirement. The other words ('candid', 'abrogates', 'insinuations') are used correctly.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: The manager's perfunctory inspection missed several obvious defects in the machinery.
The sculptor's ostensible reason for the delay was a shortage of marble.
The villagers were forced to forbear their land after the flood destroyed the embankment.
Her pithy remark summed up the entire debate in a single memorable line.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: 'Forbear' means to politely or patiently restrain oneself from doing something. The villagers were forced to abandon or give up their land, which requires the verb 'forsake' or 'forego', making 'forbear' incorrect.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: The tribunal's verdict was an unequivocal rejection of the company's claims.
The shop's meagre profits were barely enough to sustain the family.
The teacher's scathing praise encouraged the class to try harder.
The mayor's laconic reply, just three words long, ended the press conference.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: 'Scathing' means severely critical or harsh. It is a contradiction in terms to use it with 'praise' (scathing criticism would work, but not scathing praise).

questions.question: Examinations promise fairness by asking everyone the same questions. ____________________. A student who has never seen a multiple-choice format, or who reads the language of the paper as a second language, is being measured partly on something other than what the test claims to measure. Sameness of procedure, in short, is not the same as sameness of opportunity.
options: Many countries have therefore abolished written examinations in favour of continuous assessment in schools and colleges.
But identical questions do not guarantee that everyone meets them equally prepared.
Teachers generally prefer examinations because they are far easier and quicker to grade than projects or portfolios.
Examinations were first introduced in imperial China as a means of selecting civil servants for the state.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: The paragraph argues that identical testing conditions do not equate to actual fairness because of background disparities. Option 2 bridges this gap smoothly by stating that 'identical questions do not guarantee that everyone meets them equally prepared', which sets up the examples given in the subsequent sentences.

questions.question: A translator is often called a traitor, but the proverb flatters the original. ____________________. Every language divides experience differently, and a word with no counterpart forces the translator to choose between fidelity to sense and fidelity to sound. Those choices are not betrayals; they are the work itself.
options: Many classic works are today available in dozens of languages thanks to the growth of modern publishing houses.
Machine translation has recently begun to rival human translators when handling ordinary everyday texts and documents.
Poetry is generally considered the hardest genre to translate because of its heavy dependence on rhyme and metre.
It assumes that a perfect version exists and that the translator has merely failed to deliver it.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: The opening line critiques the idiom calling a translator a 'traitor'. Option 3 expands on why the proverb flatters the original: 'It assumes that a perfect version exists and that the translator has merely failed to deliver it', before refuting this illusion in the lines following.

questions.question: Cities that depend on a single industry enjoy remarkable prosperity while it lasts. ____________________. When the steel plant or the textile mill closes, the shops, schools and tax base that grew around it close with it, and the skills of the workforce are suddenly worth little. Diversification is dull in good years and invaluable in bad ones.
options: Governments in many countries have offered generous tax incentives to attract large manufacturers to small towns.
Such cities usually have better public transport and schools than those whose economies are more varied in character.
Steel and textiles were the two industries that contributed most to the industrial growth of the nineteenth century.
That prosperity, however, is a loan rather than a gift, repayable when the industry declines.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: The paragraph highlights the contrast between temporary boom and ultimate collapse in single-industry towns. Option 3 captures this dynamic using a brilliant metaphor: 'That prosperity, however, is a loan rather than a gift, repayable when the industry declines'.

questions.passage:
Karan Mehta (Host, Citywise Radio): Every monsoon, the same streets go under. Is this simply a rainfall problem?

Dr. Sunita Iyer (urban planner): Rainfall is the trigger, not the cause. Cities used to have lakes, marshes and open soil that absorbed water. We have paved over most of them, so the rain that once soaked in now runs off all at once and overwhelms drains designed for a smaller city.

Karan Mehta: So the answer is bigger drains?

Dr. Sunita Iyer: Only partly. Larger drains move the flood downstream and make it someone else's problem. The better approach is to slow the water down: restore wetlands, build permeable pavements, create retention ponds in parks.
questions.question: According to Dr. Iyer, the main cause of urban flooding is that
options: built-up cities have lost the soil and wetlands that once absorbed rainwater
monsoon rainfall has become far heavier in recent decades
existing drains are poorly maintained by city authorities
rivers and lakes are being drained to make way for farmland
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: Dr. Iyer explicitly notes that cities have 'paved over' lakes, marshes, and open soil that used to absorb water, turning natural absorption into sudden surface runoff.

wetlands are generally less effective than drains in preventing floods

questions.question:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Each sentence is labelled with a number. Decide on the most logical order and enter only the sequence of numbers in the space provided.

1. Newton showed that the moon's gravity pulls the oceans toward it, producing a bulge on the near side.
2. The resolution lies in the fact that the Earth itself is pulled toward the moon more strongly than the far-side water is, leaving that water behind.
3. Yet this explained only half the pattern, since a second bulge appears on the far side of the Earth at the same time.
4. For centuries, sailors knew that tides rose and fell twice a day without knowing why.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: Sentence 4 introduces the historical background of tides. Sentence 1 presents Newton's explanation of the near-side bulge. Sentence 3 introduces the discrepancy ('Yet this explained only half the pattern... far side'). Sentence 2 resolves the puzzle of the second bulge.

questions.question:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Each sentence is labelled with a number. Decide on the most logical order and enter only the sequence of numbers in the space provided.

1. Charles II, alarmed, tried to suppress them in 1675.
2. In seventeenth-century London, coffeehouses were called 'penny universities', since a penny bought a cup and entry into the conversation.
3. The episode shows how quickly a new place for talking could be seen as a threat to authority.
4. Men of every rank mingled there, which unsettled those who believed that talk about politics belonged to the privileged.
5. The proclamation was withdrawn within days, so strong was the public outcry.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: Sentence 2 introduces coffeehouses. Sentence 4 explains why they unsettled authorities (mixing social ranks). Sentence 1 states Charles II's attempt to suppress them. Sentence 5 notes the public backlash, and Sentence 3 concludes with the broader lesson.

questions.question:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Each sentence is labelled with a number. Decide on the most logical order and enter only the sequence of numbers in the space provided.

1. The result is that calls once audible over great distances are now masked, and some species have begun to call louder or at different pitches.
2. Whether such adjustments are enough to preserve their social lives remains unknown.
3. Sound travels farther and faster in water than in air, which is why whales rely on it to find mates across hundreds of kilometres.
4. Commercial shipping has raised the ocean's background noise sharply over the past half century.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: Sentence 3 explains how sound works for whales in water. Sentence 4 introduces the disruption caused by commercial shipping noise. Sentence 1 describes the consequences (masked calls, behavioral adjustments), and Sentence 2 questions the long-term effectiveness.

questions.question:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Each sentence is labelled with a number. Decide on the most logical order and enter only the sequence of numbers in the space provided.

1. His sentences, by his own account, became terser.
2. Whether the same is true of today's software is a question we have only begun to ask.
3. When the typewriter appeared, many writers feared it would mechanise thought.
4. Such observations suggest that tools shape the content of writing, not merely its production.
5. Nietzsche, who turned to a typing machine as his eyesight failed, noted that it seemed to change his style as well as his speed.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: Sentence 3 introduces the general historical fear regarding typewriters. Sentence 5 provides Nietzsche's specific example. Sentence 1 gives the specific effect on his writing style. Sentence 4 generalizes from this observation, and Sentence 2 extends it to modern software.

questions.question:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Each sentence is labelled with a number. Decide on the most logical order and enter only the sequence of numbers in the space provided.

1. Harvesting does not kill the plant, since new shoots rise from the same root system.
2. Timber trees, by contrast, must be felled and replanted, with decades before the next harvest.
3. Bamboo is technically a grass, yet some species grow nearly a metre in a single day.
4. This speed, combined with its strength, has made it attractive as a substitute for timber.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: Sentence 3 introduces bamboo and its rapid growth rate. Sentence 4 explains how this speed and strength make it a timber alternative. Sentence 1 explains its harvesting properties, and Sentence 2 contrasts this directly with timber trees.

questions.passage: Behavioural economists have popularised the idea of the 'nudge': a change in the way choices are presented that steers people toward better outcomes without forbidding anything. Enrolling employees in a pension scheme by default, with the freedom to opt out, is the standard illustration. Its defenders call this 'libertarian paternalism', a phrase meant to reassure both camps: nobody's options are removed, yet the architecture of choice leans in a welfare-enhancing direction. Critics respond that the reassurance is thin. Every choice must be presented somehow, so neutrality is not on offer; the real question is who selects the default and in whose interest. A government that sets the default is hardly an innocent bystander, and a firm that does so may be steering people toward its own margins rather than their welfare. There is also a subtler worry. A nudge works best when it bypasses deliberation, exploiting habit and inertia, and a policy that succeeds by circumventing reasoning sits uneasily with the ideal of citizens as reasoners. Defenders reply that people are already being nudged constantly, by supermarket layouts and app designs, and that the only choice is between nudges designed with care and nudges designed for profit. This is a fair point, but it proves less than it seems: that private actors manipulate us is an argument for restraining them, not a licence for the state to do likewise. What remains is a modest conclusion. Nudges are defensible where they are transparent, easily reversed and aligned with what people themselves would endorse on reflection, and suspect wherever they depend on being unnoticed.
questions.question: Which of the following best captures the author's conclusion about nudges?
options: Nudges are acceptable only when transparent, reversible and endorsable on reflection
Governments should abandon nudging altogether because any attempt to steer behaviour violates individual liberty and choice
Nudges are harmless, since people are already influenced by countless commercial pressures in everyday life
Default options are the most effective of all policy instruments for improving employee pension savings and welfare
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: The author's final paragraph explicitly concludes that nudges are defensible only under specific conditions: when they are transparent, easily reversed, and aligned with what individuals would reflectively endorse.

questions.passage: A map is usually taken to be a reduction of the world, a smaller and tidier copy of it. The cartographer's own training suggests the opposite: a map is an argument. Because the globe cannot be flattened without distortion, every projection chooses what to keep faithful, whether area, angle or distance, and what to sacrifice. The Mercator projection, devised for navigators who needed straight lines of constant compass bearing, enlarges regions near the poles; its later adoption in school atlases made Europe loom larger than Africa and encouraged, without anyone intending it, a quiet hierarchy of importance. Nor is the problem confined to geometry. A colonial survey that marked a river as a boundary and left a pastoral people's seasonal routes unrecorded did not merely describe a territory; it prepared the ground for who would be allowed to own it. Maps, in other words, do not follow power so much as help to make it. It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that all maps are propaganda and that the search for accuracy is naive. A railway diagram that abandons geography to make connections clear is not lying; it is answering the traveller's question. The sensible lesson is to ask of any map what it was drawn to help someone do, and what that purpose led its maker to leave out.
questions.question: The central claim of the passage is that
options: accurate maps are impossible to produce, so the pursuit of cartographic accuracy should be abandoned altogether by modern societies
colonial surveys were the main source of the distortion in the maps later used in schools around the world
maps embody choices and purposes, so they should be read as arguments, not neutral copies
the Mercator projection should be replaced in school atlases by projections that preserve the true size of every region

questions.passage: A map is usually taken to be a reduction of the world, a smaller and tidier copy of it. The cartographer's own training suggests the opposite: a map is an argument. Because the globe cannot be flattened without distortion, every projection chooses what to keep faithful, whether area, angle or distance, and what to sacrifice. The Mercator projection, devised for navigators who needed straight lines of constant compass bearing, enlarges regions near the poles; its later adoption in school atlases made Europe loom larger than Africa and encouraged, without anyone intending it, a quiet hierarchy of importance. Nor is the problem confined to geometry. A colonial survey that marked a river as a boundary and left a pastoral people's seasonal routes unrecorded did not merely describe a territory; it prepared the ground for who would be allowed to own it. Maps, in other words, do not follow power so much as help to make it. It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that all maps are propaganda and that the search for accuracy is naive. A railway diagram that abandons geography to make connections clear is not lying; it is answering the traveller's question. The sensible lesson is to ask of any map what it was drawn to help someone do, and what that purpose led its maker to leave out.
questions.question: The passage mentions the Mercator projection primarily to show that

navigators deliberately designed the projection to exaggerate the importance of European countries over African ones
school atlases are the only context in which cartographic distortion has practical consequences for ordinary readers
straight lines of constant compass bearing are impossible to represent on any flat map of the globe
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: Mercator designed it for navigation, but its use in school atlases created an unintended visual hierarchy (making Europe loom larger than Africa).

questions.passage: The great nineteenth-century naturalists could, with some exaggeration, claim to know a whole science. Today a physicist may never read a paper outside a sub-subfield of a few hundred people. Specialisation is usually defended as the price of progress: knowledge has grown so vast that depth is possible only by narrowing. The defence is largely correct, yet it hides a cost that is easy to overlook because it does not appear in any single paper. Problems that matter rarely respect the boundaries of departments. Antibiotic resistance is at once a problem of microbiology, economics and hospital administration, and no specialist is trained to see all three at once. The usual response is the interdisciplinary team, but teams bring their own difficulties: members must spend so much effort translating between vocabularies that little remains for original thought, and credit tends to flow to the home discipline of the most senior member. A better remedy may be less glamorous. It is to ensure that a few researchers are rewarded for being broad rather than deep: people who read widely, connect findings across fields and ask questions no specialist would think to ask. Such people will rarely produce the sharpest result in any one area. Their value lies in noticing that two areas are secretly asking the same question, something the specialists, absorbed in their own corner, are least likely to see.
questions.question: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
options: Specialisation has been a mistake, and science should return to the nineteenth-century model of the universal naturalist
Interdisciplinary teams are the best solution to the problems created by increasing specialisation in modern science
Knowledge has grown too vast for any researcher to make a meaningful contribution outside a narrow subfield
Narrow specialisation carries a hidden cost, which rewarding some broad researchers could help offset
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: The passage acknowledges the necessity of specialization while highlighting its hidden cost (cross-disciplinary blindness) and proposes rewarding generalist, broad thinkers as a corrective remedy.
